category: Symbolic Math Toolbox > Core Symbolic Computation
description: Declaring symbolic variables and functions, algebraic manipulation, equation and ODE solving, calculus, integral transforms, vector calculus, variable-precision arithmetic and conversion to numeric MATLAB code.

tools.name: syms
tools.description: Declare one or more symbolic variables or symbolic functions in the workspace in a compact command form. Assumptions such as real, positive or integer can be attached at declaration, which lets simplify produce much stronger results. This is the normal way to start any symbolic computation.
tools.usage:
syms x y z
syms x real
syms n positive integer
syms f(x) g(x, y)
syms A [3 3] matrix

parameters.name: f(x)
parameters.description: Parenthesized form declares a symbolic function of the given arguments.

parameters.name: [m n]
parameters.description: Creates a symbolic matrix of named elements.

tools.example:
syms x y real
syms n positive integer
syms f(t)
expr = sqrt(x^2);
simplify(expr)             % abs(x) because x is real
f(t) = exp(-t)*sin(t);
disp(diff(f, t))
tools.notes: syms clears any previous value and assumptions for those names. Use assume/assumptions to inspect or add constraints later.

tools.name: sym
tools.description: Create a symbolic number, variable, expression or matrix as a function call, which allows programmatic construction that the syms command cannot do. Converting a numeric value with sym gives an exact rational or symbolic constant rather than a floating-point approximation. Use the 'f', 'r', 'e' or 'd' flags to control how doubles are converted.
tools.usage:
S = sym(num)
S = sym(num, flag)
S = sym('x')
S = sym('x', assumption)
S = sym('a', [2 3])

parameters.name: num
parameters.description: A numeric value, array, or a character string to parse.

parameters.name: [m n]
parameters.description: Create an m-by-n matrix of indexed symbols.

tools.notes: sym(0.1) gives exactly 1/10 by default; sym(0.1,'f') shows what the double really holds.

tools.name: simplify
tools.description: Apply a broad set of algebraic and trigonometric simplification rules to reduce a symbolic expression. The Steps option lets it try harder at the cost of time, and IgnoreAnalyticConstraints allows transformations that are valid only generically. Simplification is heuristic, so try simplify, combine, rewrite and expand when the first result is unsatisfying.
tools.usage:
S = simplify(expr)
S = simplify(expr, Name, Value)

parameters.name: 'Steps'
parameters.description: Number of simplification passes (default 1); higher often finds a shorter form.

parameters.name: 'IgnoreAnalyticConstraints'
parameters.description: Logical; apply rules like log(a*b) = log a + log b without branch checks.

tools.example:
syms x
expr = (cos(x)^2 - sin(x)^2) / (cos(x) + sin(x));
simplify(expr)                               % cos(x) - sin(x)
simplify(sqrt(x^2 + 2*x + 1), 'Steps', 20)
simplify(log(exp(x)), 'IgnoreAnalyticConstraints', true)

tools.name: expand
tools.description: Expand products, powers and compositions of functions into sums of terms, including trigonometric addition formulas and logarithm/exponential rules. It is the natural counterpart to factor and collect. Use ArithmeticOnly to expand polynomials without touching trigonometric or transcendental functions.
tools.usage:
S = expand(expr)
S = expand(expr, Name, Value)

parameters.name: 'ArithmeticOnly'
parameters.description: Logical; expand only arithmetic operations, leaving sin, log etc. alone.

tools.example:
syms x y
expand((x + y)^4)
expand(sin(x + y))                    % cos(x)*sin(y) + cos(y)*sin(x)
expand(log(x*y), 'IgnoreAnalyticConstraints', true)
expand(cos(3*x), 'ArithmeticOnly', true)

tools.name: factor
tools.description: Factor a symbolic polynomial into irreducible factors, or factor an integer into primes. The FactorMode option controls the field over which factorization is attempted, allowing complex or arbitrary algebraic-extension factors. Use it to find roots structurally and to simplify rational expressions.
tools.usage:
F = factor(expr)
F = factor(n)
F = factor(expr, vars)
F = factor(___, 'FactorMode', mode)

parameters.name: expr
parameters.description: Symbolic polynomial or integer to factor.

parameters.name: vars
parameters.description: Variables with respect to which to factor.

tools.example:
syms x
factor(x^3 - 6*x^2 + 11*x - 6)          % [x-1, x-2, x-3]
factor(x^2 + 1, 'FactorMode', 'complex')
factor(sym(1234567890))
prod(factor(x^4 - 1))
tools.notes: For polynomials factor returns a vector of factors, so use prod() to rebuild the product.

tools.name: collect
tools.description: Collect coefficients of like powers of a specified variable, rewriting an expression as a polynomial in that variable. This is how you extract the structure of an expression with respect to one symbol while treating the others as parameters. Pass a vector of variables to collect successively.
tools.usage:
S = collect(expr)
S = collect(expr, var)
S = collect(expr, vars)
tools.example:
syms x a b
expr = a*x^2 + b*x^2 + 3*x - a*x + 7;
collect(expr, x)                         % (a + b)*x^2 + (3 - a)*x + 7
c = coeffs(collect(expr, x), x, 'All')

tools.name: rewrite
tools.description: Rewrite an expression in terms of a different function family, for example trigonometric functions as exponentials, or tan as sin/cos. It is often the key step when simplify alone cannot bridge two representations. Supported targets include exp, log, sincos, sin, cos, tan, sqrt, heaviside and piecewise.
tools.usage: S = rewrite(expr, target)
tools.example:
syms x
rewrite(cos(x), 'exp')
rewrite(tan(x), 'sincos')
rewrite(abs(x), 'piecewise')
simplify(rewrite(sin(x)^2 + cos(x)^2, 'exp'))

tools.name: subs
tools.description: Substitute values or expressions for symbolic variables. It accepts scalars, vectors of variables with matching values, or a structure returned by solve. Substituting numeric values still gives a symbolic result, so wrap in double or vpa when you want a number.
tools.usage:
snew = subs(s, new)
snew = subs(s, old, new)
snew = subs(s, {old1, old2}, {new1, new2})
snew = subs(s, solutionStruct)
tools.example:
syms x y
f = x^2 + y^2;
subs(f, x, 3)                              % 9 + y^2
subs(f, [x y], [3 4])                      % 25
double(subs(f, {x, y}, {sym(pi), 1}))
sol = solve(x^2 - 5*x + 6 == 0, x);
subs(x^3, x, sol)
tools.notes: subs does not evaluate numerically; follow with double() or vpa() to get a number.

tools.name: solve
tools.description: Solve symbolic equations or systems of equations analytically for the specified unknowns. It returns a symbolic array for a single unknown or a structure with one field per unknown for systems. Options control whether to return parameters and conditions, restrict to real solutions, or fall back to numeric solving.
tools.usage:
S = solve(eqn, var)
S = solve(eqns, vars)
[y1, y2] = solve(eqns, [x1 x2])
S = solve(___, Name, Value)

parameters.name: eqn / eqns
parameters.description: Equation(s) using == , or expressions assumed equal to zero.

parameters.name: 'ReturnConditions'
parameters.description: Logical; also return parameters and the conditions under which solutions are valid.

parameters.name: 'MaxDegree'
parameters.description: Maximum polynomial degree for explicit radical solutions (default 2, up to 4).

parameters.name: 'PrincipalValue'
parameters.description: Logical; return only one solution of a periodic equation.

tools.notes: If solve returns an empty result the system may have no closed form; try vpasolve for a numeric answer.

tools.name: vpasolve
tools.description: Solve equations numerically with variable-precision arithmetic, which works when no closed-form solution exists. For polynomial systems it finds all roots; for nonpolynomial ones it returns one solution near an initial guess or inside a specified search range. Use 'Random' with a loop to hunt for multiple solutions.
tools.usage:
S = vpasolve(eqn)
S = vpasolve(eqn, var)
S = vpasolve(eqn, var, init_guess)
S = vpasolve(eqns, vars, Name, Value)

parameters.name: init_guess
parameters.description: Starting point, or a two-element interval [lo hi] to search.

parameters.name: 'Random'
parameters.description: Logical; use random starting points, useful in a loop to find several roots.

tools.example:
syms x
vpasolve(x^5 - 3*x + 1 == 0, x)           % all five roots
vpasolve(cos(x) == x, x, 0.7)
vpasolve(exp(x) == 3*x, x, [0 1])
digits(30); vpasolve(x^2 == 2, x)

tools.name: dsolve
tools.description: Solve ordinary differential equations and systems of ODEs analytically, with optional initial or boundary conditions. Derivatives are written with diff on a symbolic function such as y(t). If no closed form exists it returns an empty result, in which case you should switch to a numeric solver like ode45.
tools.usage:
S = dsolve(eqn)
S = dsolve(eqn, cond)
S = dsolve(eqns, conds)
S = dsolve(___, 'IgnoreAnalyticConstraints', tf)

parameters.name: eqn
parameters.description: Differential equation built from diff(y, t) and diff(y, t, 2).

parameters.name: cond
parameters.description: Initial or boundary conditions such as y(0) == 1, Dy(0) == 0.

parameters.name: 'IgnoreAnalyticConstraints'
parameters.description: Allow generically valid simplifications during solving.

tools.notes: Use odeToVectorField plus matlabFunction to hand a symbolic ODE to ode45 when no analytic solution exists.

tools.name: odeToVectorField
tools.description: Convert a higher-order symbolic ODE (or system) into an equivalent first-order vector field, which is the form the numeric ode solvers require. It returns the vector field and the substitution map telling you what each state variable means. Combine it with matlabFunction to produce a function handle for ode45.
tools.usage:
V = odeToVectorField(eqns)
[V, S] = odeToVectorField(eqns)

parameters.name: eqns
parameters.description: One or more symbolic differential equations.

parameters.name: V
parameters.description: Symbolic vector field in the variable Y.

parameters.name: S
parameters.description: Vector showing which original quantity each element of Y represents.

tools.name: diff
tools.description: Compute symbolic derivatives of any order with respect to one or more variables. With several variables it computes mixed partial derivatives in the order given. It is the basis of symbolic Jacobians, gradients and Taylor expansions.
tools.usage:
Df = diff(f)
Df = diff(f, var)
Df = diff(f, n)
Df = diff(f, var, n)
Df = diff(f, var1, var2)

parameters.name: var
parameters.description: Differentiation variable; defaults to the one returned by symvar.

tools.example:
syms x y
f = x^3 * sin(y) + exp(x*y);
diff(f, x)
diff(f, x, 2)
diff(f, x, y)                       % mixed partial
syms g(x)
diff(g(x)^2, x)                     % chain rule with an unknown function

tools.name: int
tools.description: Compute indefinite or definite symbolic integrals. Definite integration accepts infinite limits and can return conditional results with assumptions on parameters. If no closed form exists it returns the unevaluated integral, which you can then evaluate numerically with vpaintegral or integral.
tools.usage:
F = int(expr)
F = int(expr, var)
F = int(expr, a, b)
F = int(expr, var, a, b)
F = int(___, Name, Value)

parameters.name: a, b
parameters.description: Integration limits, which may be -Inf and Inf.

parameters.name: 'PrincipalValue'
parameters.description: Logical; return the Cauchy principal value.

parameters.name: 'Hold'
parameters.description: Logical; return the integral unevaluated for display.

tools.example:
syms x a positive
int(x^2 * exp(-a*x), x)
int(exp(-a*x^2), x, -Inf, Inf)          % sqrt(pi/a)
int(sin(x)/x, x, 0, Inf)                % pi/2
vpa(int(exp(-x^2)*log(x), x, 1, 2), 12)

tools.name: limit
tools.description: Compute the limit of a symbolic expression as a variable approaches a value, optionally from the left or the right. It handles limits at infinity and indeterminate forms that require L'Hopital's rule. Use it to analyse asymptotic behaviour and removable singularities.
tools.usage:
L = limit(f, var, a)
L = limit(f, a)
L = limit(f, var, a, 'left')
L = limit(f, var, a, 'right')

parameters.name: var
parameters.description: Variable that approaches the limit point.

parameters.name: a
parameters.description: Limit point; can be Inf or -Inf.

tools.example:
syms x n
limit(sin(x)/x, x, 0)                 % 1
limit((1 + 1/n)^n, n, Inf)            % exp(1)
limit(1/x, x, 0, 'right')             % Inf
limit(1/x, x, 0, 'left')              % -Inf

tools.name: taylor
tools.description: Compute the Taylor (or Laurent/Puiseux) series expansion of an expression about a point, truncated at a given order. Multivariate expansions are supported by passing a vector of variables and expansion points. Use it to derive approximations, linearize models and analyse local behaviour.
tools.usage:
T = taylor(f)
T = taylor(f, var)
T = taylor(f, var, a)
T = taylor(f, var, 'Order', n)
T = taylor(f, vars, as, Name, Value)

parameters.name: 'Order'
parameters.description: Truncation order n; terms up to degree n-1 are kept (default 6).

tools.example:
syms x y
taylor(exp(x), x, 'Order', 6)
taylor(log(x), x, 1, 'Order', 5)
T = taylor(sin(x)*cos(y), [x y], [0 0], 'Order', 4);
fplot([sin(x), taylor(sin(x), x, 'Order', 8)], [-6 6])
tools.notes: 'Order', n keeps terms of degree less than n, so 'Order', 6 gives degrees 0 through 5.

tools.name: symsum
tools.description: Evaluate a symbolic sum in closed form, either indefinite (an antidifference) or over a definite range including infinite ranges. It can prove and evaluate classic series such as geometric and Basel sums. Use it to derive formulas rather than compute numerically.
tools.usage:
F = symsum(f, k)
F = symsum(f, k, a, b)
F = symsum(f, a, b)

parameters.name: a, b
parameters.description: Lower and upper limits; b may be Inf.

tools.example:
syms k n x
symsum(k, k, 1, n)                     % n*(n+1)/2
symsum(1/k^2, k, 1, Inf)               % pi^2/6
symsum(x^k, k, 0, Inf)                 % 1/(1-x) with |x| < 1
symsum(k^3, k, 1, n)

tools.name: symprod
tools.description: Evaluate a symbolic product in closed form over a definite or indefinite range. It recognizes products that reduce to factorials, gamma functions and Pochhammer symbols. Use it for combinatorial identities and infinite-product evaluations.
tools.usage:
F = symprod(f, k)
F = symprod(f, k, a, b)
F = symprod(f, a, b)

parameters.name: a, b
parameters.description: Lower and upper limits; b may be Inf.

tools.example:
syms k n
symprod(k, k, 1, n)                     % factorial(n)
symprod(1 - 1/k^2, k, 2, Inf)           % 1/2
simplify(symprod(k/(k+1), k, 1, n))

tools.name: laplace
tools.description: Compute the one-sided Laplace transform of a symbolic expression, turning differential equations into algebraic ones. Default variables are t for time and s for the transform domain. It is the core tool for classical control and circuit analysis in the symbolic workflow.
tools.usage:
F = laplace(f)
F = laplace(f, transVar)
F = laplace(f, var, transVar)
tools.example:
syms t s a positive
laplace(exp(-a*t))                      % 1/(a+s)
laplace(t^2*sin(3*t))
laplace(heaviside(t-2)*cos(t), t, s)
syms y(t)
laplace(diff(y, t, 2), t, s)

tools.name: ilaplace
tools.description: Compute the inverse Laplace transform, returning a time-domain expression from a transfer function or transformed equation. Rational functions are handled by partial-fraction expansion, producing exponentials, sinusoids and Heaviside/Dirac terms. Use it to get the analytic step or impulse response of a system.
tools.usage:
f = ilaplace(F)
f = ilaplace(F, transVar)
f = ilaplace(F, var, transVar)

tools.name: fourier
tools.description: Compute the continuous Fourier transform of a symbolic expression, using the angular-frequency convention with default variables x and w. It handles Dirac deltas, Heaviside steps and Gaussians analytically. Use it for analytic spectral analysis and for deriving transform pairs.
tools.usage:
F = fourier(f)
F = fourier(f, transVar)
F = fourier(f, var, transVar)

parameters.name: var
parameters.description: Original variable (default x, or the symvar result).

tools.example:
syms t w a positive
fourier(exp(-a*t^2), t, w)
fourier(exp(-a*abs(t)), t, w)
fourier(heaviside(t)*exp(-a*t), t, w)
fourier(dirac(t), t, w)                 % 1
tools.notes: MATLAB uses F(w) = int(f(t)*exp(-1i*w*t), t, -Inf, Inf); other texts use different normalizations.

tools.name: ifourier
tools.description: Compute the inverse continuous Fourier transform, recovering the original function from its spectrum. It uses the 1/(2*pi) normalization matching MATLAB's fourier. Use it to verify transform pairs and to derive impulse responses from frequency responses.
tools.usage:
f = ifourier(F)
f = ifourier(F, transVar)
f = ifourier(F, var, transVar)
tools.example:
syms w t a positive
F = 2*a/(a^2 + w^2);
simplify(ifourier(F, w, t))             % exp(-a*abs(t))
ifourier(exp(-w^2), w, t)

tools.name: ztrans
tools.description: Compute the one-sided Z-transform of a discrete-time symbolic sequence, with default variables n and z. It turns difference equations into algebraic equations, which is the discrete analogue of the Laplace transform. Use it for digital filter and discrete control analysis.
tools.usage:
F = ztrans(f)
F = ztrans(f, transVar)
F = ztrans(f, var, transVar)
tools.example:
syms n z a
ztrans(a^n, n, z)                       % z/(z-a)
ztrans(n*a^n, n, z)
ztrans(cos(3*n), n, z)
ztrans(kroneckerDelta(n), n, z)         % 1

tools.name: iztrans
tools.description: Compute the inverse Z-transform, returning a closed-form sequence from a transfer function in z. Rational functions are expanded into geometric and polynomial terms. Use it to obtain the analytic impulse response of a digital filter.
tools.usage:
f = iztrans(F)
f = iztrans(F, transVar)
f = iztrans(F, var, transVar)

tools.name: jacobian
tools.description: Compute the Jacobian matrix of a vector-valued function with respect to a vector of variables. Each row is the gradient of one component function. It is essential for Newton methods, sensitivity analysis and linearizing nonlinear state-space models.
tools.usage:
J = jacobian(f, v)
J = jacobian(f)

parameters.name: v
parameters.description: Vector of variables to differentiate with respect to.

tools.name: hessian
tools.description: Compute the Hessian matrix of second partial derivatives of a scalar function. Its eigenvalues classify stationary points as minima, maxima or saddle points. Newton-type optimization methods use it directly.
tools.usage:
H = hessian(f, v)
H = hessian(f)

tools.name: gradient
tools.description: Compute the symbolic gradient vector of a scalar field with respect to a list of variables. It is a convenience wrapper around jacobian for scalar functions, returning a column vector. Use it for optimality conditions and for building analytic gradients to pass to fmincon.
tools.usage:
g = gradient(f, v)
g = gradient(f)

tools.name: divergence
tools.description: Compute the divergence of a symbolic vector field, the scalar measure of how much the field spreads from a point. It is central to continuity equations, Gauss's law and fluid dynamics. Pass the field and the coordinate variables in matching order.
tools.usage:
d = divergence(V, X)
d = divergence(V)

tools.name: curl
tools.description: Compute the curl of a symbolic 3-D vector field, measuring its local rotation. A zero curl means the field is conservative and has a scalar potential. Used throughout electromagnetics and fluid mechanics.
tools.usage:
c = curl(V, X)
c = curl(V)

tools.name: vpa
tools.description: Evaluate a symbolic expression in variable-precision floating-point arithmetic with a specified number of significant digits. Unlike double it can carry hundreds of digits, which is essential for ill-conditioned problems and for studying round-off. Results remain symbolic objects, displayed to the requested precision.
tools.usage:
y = vpa(x)
y = vpa(x, d)

parameters.name: d
parameters.description: Number of significant digits; defaults to the current digits setting (32).

tools.example:
vpa(pi, 50)
vpa(sym(1)/3, 40)
syms x
vpa(subs(exp(x)*sin(x), x, sym(1)), 25)
vpa(exp(sym(1)) - exp(1), 20)   % shows double round-off
tools.notes: vpa(0.1) shows the double's actual value; vpa(sym(1)/10) shows an exact tenth.

tools.name: digits
tools.description: Query or set the default number of significant decimal digits used by variable-precision arithmetic. It affects every subsequent vpa and vpasolve call in the session. Save the old value and restore it to keep changes local to a function.
tools.usage:
digits(d)
d = digits
oldDigits = digits(d)

tools.name: matlabFunction
tools.description: Convert a symbolic expression, vector or matrix into an anonymous function handle or a generated MATLAB function file. This is the bridge from symbolic derivation to fast numeric evaluation with ode45, fmincon, fsolve or plotting. Use 'Vars' to fix the argument order and 'File' to write a reusable .m file.
tools.usage:
ht = matlabFunction(f)
ht = matlabFunction(f1, f2, ...)
matlabFunction(f, 'File', filename)
ht = matlabFunction(___, 'Vars', vars, 'Outputs', names)

parameters.name: 'Vars'
parameters.description: Cell or vector fixing the order and grouping of input arguments.

parameters.name: 'File'
parameters.description: Name of the generated function file; omit for an anonymous handle.

parameters.name: 'Optimize'
parameters.description: Logical (default true when writing a file); factor out common subexpressions.

tools.notes: Generated code uses element-wise operators, so the handle works on arrays as well as scalars.

tools.name: latex
tools.description: Convert a symbolic expression into a LaTeX string for use in publications, titles and annotations. The result can be dropped straight into a document or into MATLAB's own LaTeX-aware text interpreter. Combine with title(...,'Interpreter','latex') to label figures with typeset formulas.
tools.usage: str = latex(S)
tools.example:
syms x
f = int(exp(-x^2), x, 0, Inf);
s = latex(f)
fplot(sin(x)/x, [-10 10])
title(['$' latex(sin(x)/x) '$'], 'Interpreter', 'latex', 'FontSize', 14)

tools.name: equationsToMatrix
tools.description: Convert a system of linear symbolic equations into coefficient matrix and right-hand-side vector form A*x = b. It validates that the equations really are linear in the chosen variables. Feed its outputs to linsolve or to the backslash operator.
tools.usage:
[A, b] = equationsToMatrix(eqns, vars)
[A, b] = equationsToMatrix(eqns)
A = equationsToMatrix(eqns, vars)

parameters.name: eqns
parameters.description: Vector of linear symbolic equations or expressions.

parameters.name: vars
parameters.description: Variables to treat as unknowns; everything else becomes a parameter.

tools.name: linsolve
tools.description: Solve a symbolic linear system A*x = B exactly, returning parametric solutions when the system is underdetermined. The second output gives the parameters introduced for free variables. It warns when the system is inconsistent or the matrix is singular.
tools.usage:
X = linsolve(A, B)
[X, R] = linsolve(A, B)

parameters.name: R
parameters.description: Reciprocal condition number, or the parameters in a parametric solution.

tools.name: assume
tools.description: Impose assumptions on symbolic variables, such as being real, positive, integer or satisfying an inequality, replacing any previous assumptions on them. Assumptions let simplify, solve and int produce much cleaner results and correct branch choices. Use assumeAlso to add without replacing, and assumptions to inspect what is in force.
tools.usage:
assume(condition)
assume(expr, set)
assumeAlso(condition)
assumptions
assume(x, 'clear')

parameters.name: condition
parameters.description: An inequality or logical condition, e.g. x > 0 or in(n, 'integer').

tools.example:
syms x n
assume(x > 0)
simplify(sqrt(x^2))                  % x, not abs(x)
assume(n, 'integer')
assumeAlso(n > 0)
disp(assumptions)
simplify(sin(n*pi))                  % 0
assume([x n], 'clear')
tools.notes: Assumptions persist in the workspace until cleared; forgetting to clear them is a common source of surprising results.

tools.name: isAlways
tools.description: Test whether a symbolic condition holds for all values consistent with the current assumptions, returning a logical rather than a symbolic result. Ordinary comparison of symbolic expressions returns an unevaluated condition, so isAlways is how you get a true/false answer. Options control what happens when the condition cannot be decided.
tools.usage:
tf = isAlways(cond)
tf = isAlways(cond, Name, Value)

parameters.name: cond
parameters.description: Symbolic condition or array of conditions.

tools.example:
syms x
assume(x > 2)
isAlways(x^2 > 4)                             % true
isAlways(sin(x)^2 + cos(x)^2 == 1)            % true
isAlways(x > 5, 'Unknown', 'false')           % false rather than an error
